blocks.content: Most developers learn that a class should be small, but "small" is a surprisingly vague rule.

["Is a 50-line class small? 
","What about 500 lines? 
"]
items: Is a 50-line class small?
What about 500 lines?

blocks.content: In practice, class size alone tells us very little about whether a design is good or bad. Some tiny classes are responsible for several unrelated concerns, while some larger classes remain focused on a single well-defined job.

The real measure of a healthy class is not the number of methods or lines of code it contains. The real measure is responsibility. A well-designed class has a clear purpose, a clear reason to exist, and a clear reason to change. When that focus is lost, complexity starts to grow. The class becomes harder to understand, harder to test, and harder to modify without accidentally breaking something else.
1. Why Class Size Matters

Every class is a container, and like any container, it can hold the right amount, too little, or too much. The goal is not to make classes as small as possible, but to ensure they contain a single, well-defined responsibility.

The challenge is that classes rarely become large because someone planned them that way. Instead, they grow gradually. A new feature is added, then another, then a small utility method, and eventually the class starts doing several unrelated jobs. This process is so gradual that the problem often goes unnoticed.

A developer who understands class design should be able to look at any class and quickly determine whether it has a healthy scope or whether it has started accumulating responsibilities that belong elsewhere.

blocks.content: 2. What "Responsibility" Actually Means
Before discussing class size, we need to understand what a responsibility is. A responsibility is simply a reason for a class to change.
Good Example: One Responsibility

For example, a PricingEngine class is responsible for pricing logic. If the business changes how prices are calculated, this class must change. That is one responsibility and one reason to modify the class.
Bad Example: Multiple Responsibilities

Problems begin when a class has multiple unrelated reasons to change. Imagine a class that calculates prices, sends emails, and stores data in a database. Now a change in pricing rules, a change in the email provider, or a change in the database schema could all require modifications to the same class.
Those are unrelated concerns, which means the class has multiple responsibilities.

blocks.content: 3. The Stakeholder Test
A practical way to identify responsibilities is to think about stakeholders.

Every responsibility usually belongs to a different person, team, or business area. Pricing rules might belong to the finance team. Email templates might belong to marketing. Database structure might belong to the infrastructure team.
Now look at a class and ask: How many different stakeholders would have a valid reason to request changes to this class?

["If only one stakeholder would request changes, the class likely has a single responsibility.
","If multiple unrelated stakeholders could request changes, the class is probably doing too much.
"]
items: If only one stakeholder would request changes, the class likely has a single responsibility.
If multiple unrelated stakeholders could request changes, the class is probably doing too much.

blocks.content: This test works even when the class is small. A class can be only a few dozen lines long and still violate the Single Responsibility Principle if it serves multiple unrelated concerns.
4. How Classes Become God Objects
A God Object rarely appears overnight. Almost no developer intentionally creates a class that handles everything. Instead, it usually begins as a small, focused class with a clear responsibility.

Consider an OrderService that initially contains only order-processing logic. A new requirement arrives, and adding the code to the existing class seems convenient because all the necessary data is already available. Later, another related feature is added for the same reason. Then another. And another.

Each individual change appears reasonable when viewed in isolation. The problem is that these small additions accumulate over time. What started as a focused class gradually becomes responsible for pricing, discounts, database operations, email notifications, invoice generation, auditing, and more.
The result is a class that knows too much and does too much. Such classes are commonly called God Objects because they end up controlling many unrelated parts of the system.

The dangerous part is that there is rarely a single moment when the design suddenly becomes bad. The class grows through dozens of small decisions, each of which seems harmless at the time. By the time the problem becomes obvious, the class has already become difficult to understand, difficult to test, and difficult to modify safely.

A useful warning sign is when a class starts attracting methods that belong to different domains. If a single class is responsible for business rules, persistence, notifications, reporting, and auditing, it is no longer serving one responsibility. It has become a collection of many responsibilities that happened to accumulate in the same place.
5. Size Is a Symptom

A class should be judged by the number of responsibilities it has, not by the number of lines it contains. Line count can be a useful warning sign, but it does not determine whether a class is well designed.

["Count responsibilities, not lines: A 400-line class with one responsibility can be healthy, while a 60-line class with multiple responsibilities can be poorly designed.
","Count reasons to change: The real measure of class size is how many independent reasons the class might need to change.
","Count stakeholders: Ask who would request changes to the class. If finance, compliance, and infrastructure teams can all independently request changes, the class likely has multiple responsibilities.
","Watch the dependency list: A class importing database, email, PDF, and HTTP libraries is often handling several unrelated concerns.
","Look for unrelated methods: Methods dealing with persistence, notifications, reporting, and business rules in the same class are a strong sign of responsibility creep.
","Use line count as a warning signal: Large classes deserve inspection, but size alone does not prove a design problem.
","Small classes can still be bad: A class can be short and still violate the Single Responsibility Principle if it mixes unrelated concerns.
","Large classes can still be good: A class may contain hundreds of lines yet remain healthy if everything serves the same responsibility.
"]
items: Count responsibilities, not lines: A 400-line class with one responsibility can be healthy, while a 60-line class with multiple responsibilities can be poorly designed.
Count reasons to change: The real measure of class size is how many independent reasons the class might need to change.
Count stakeholders: Ask who would request changes to the class. If finance, compliance, and infrastructure teams can all independently request changes, the class likely has multiple responsibilities.
Watch the dependency list: A class importing database, email, PDF, and HTTP libraries is often handling several unrelated concerns.
Look for unrelated methods: Methods dealing with persistence, notifications, reporting, and business rules in the same class are a strong sign of responsibility creep.
Use line count as a warning signal: Large classes deserve inspection, but size alone does not prove a design problem.
Small classes can still be bad: A class can be short and still violate the Single Responsibility Principle if it mixes unrelated concerns.
Large classes can still be good: A class may contain hundreds of lines yet remain healthy if everything serves the same responsibility.

blocks.content: 6. Recognizing an Overgrown Class

A class rarely announces that it has become too large or taken on too many responsibilities. Instead, it leaves behind warning signs. Learning to recognize these signals helps catch design problems before they become difficult to fix.
1. The Constructor Needs Too Many Dependencies
blocks.text: 1. The Constructor Needs Too Many Dependencies

blocks.content: When a class requires a database connection, an email service, a PDF generator, a cache, and a logger just to be created, it is often a sign that the class is handling multiple jobs.
Each dependency usually represents a separate concern. The more unrelated dependencies a class needs, the more likely it is accumulating responsibilities that belong elsewhere.
2. Method Names Stop Sharing a Common Vocabulary
blocks.text: 2. Method Names Stop Sharing a Common Vocabulary

blocks.content: In a healthy class, method names usually revolve around the same concept.
An Order class might contain methods such as addItem, removeItem, calculateTotal, and applyDiscount. All of these methods belong to the same domain and speak the same language.

Problems appear when method names start belonging to completely different domains. A class containing calculateTotal, sendEmail, generatePdf, and writeAuditLog is serving multiple responsibilities. The mixed vocabulary is often a clear signal that the class has outgrown its original purpose.
3. Only Part of the Class Changes for a Feature
blocks.text: 3. Only Part of the Class Changes for a Feature

blocks.content: When a new feature request arrives, notice how much of the class is actually involved.

If adding a new payment provider consistently affects only three methods while the remaining nine methods are untouched, those methods may not belong in the same class. The class is behaving like several smaller classes that happen to share a file.
A well-focused class tends to change as a whole because its methods support the same responsibility.

blocks.content: 4. Tests Require Excessive Setup
Test complexity is often a reflection of design complexity.

If testing a simple calculation requires mocking a database, an email service, a PDF generator, and several other dependencies, the calculation logic is trapped inside a class carrying many unrelated responsibilities.
Well-designed classes are easier to test because they contain fewer concerns and require fewer collaborators.
7. Measuring Responsibility More Formally
The ideas in this lesson are not just opinions. Software engineering has formal metrics that measure the same thing.
Most of these metrics focus on cohesion and try to answer a simple question: Does this class have one responsibility, or several unrelated ones?
When a tool reports low cohesion, it is often a sign that the class has accumulated too many responsibilities.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/1782030222012-142963490.png

These tools exist because "does this feel like too much" is a judgment call that benefits from a second, numeric opinion but the underlying question they're all measuring is the same one this lesson opened with: how many genuinely separate reasons does this class have to change?
8. Walking Through an Extraction
Finding an oversized class is only half the job. The real challenge is breaking it apart without changing its behavior. Fortunately, this is usually a mechanical process rather than a creative one.
Consider the following OrderService. Over time, it has accumulated multiple responsibilities including pricing, persistence, notifications, invoice generation, and auditing.
The first step is to identify methods that naturally belong together.calculateTotal()andapplyDiscount()are both pricing-related methods.
They share the same purpose and change for the same reasons, so they can be extracted into a dedicatedPricingEngine.

The remaining methods each represent a separate responsibility. Saving orders belongs in a repository, sending emails belongs in a notification service, generating invoices belongs in an invoice generator, and audit logging belongs in an audit service.
Once these responsibilities have been extracted, the originalOrderServiceno longer performs all the work itself. Instead, it coordinates the specialized classes.
Notice what changed. The original class was responsible for five different jobs. The final version has only one responsibility:
Coordinating the order workflow.
This is the general extraction process:
["Find methods that share the same responsibility.","Move them into a dedicated class.","Extract remaining responsibilities one by one.","Leave only orchestration logic behind."]
items: Find methods that share the same responsibility.
Move them into a dedicated class.
Extract remaining responsibilities one by one.
Leave only orchestration logic behind.

blocks.content: The goal is not to create more classes. The goal is to ensure that every class has a single, clear responsibility and a single reason to change.
9. Classes That Are Too Small

Most design problems come from classes that do too much, but it is also possible to go too far in the opposite direction. Splitting every tiny piece of logic into its own class can create unnecessary complexity, making the code harder to navigate and understand.
1. Signs a Class Is Too Small
blocks.text: 1. Signs a Class Is Too Small

blocks.content: The class contains only one simple method.

["It is used from only one place in the codebase.
","It always changes together with another specific class.
","It cannot be understood without immediately opening another class.
","It exists only because \"everything should be a class\" was followed as a rule.
"]
items: It is used from only one place in the codebase.
It always changes together with another specific class.
It cannot be understood without immediately opening another class.
It exists only because "everything should be a class" was followed as a rule.

blocks.content: 2. When to Merge Classes

["Two classes always change together for the same reason.
","The abstraction provides no real testing, flexibility, or reuse benefits.
","Understanding one concept always requires opening multiple files.
","The split adds indirection but no additional clarity.
"]
items: Two classes always change together for the same reason.
The abstraction provides no real testing, flexibility, or reuse benefits.
Understanding one concept always requires opening multiple files.
The split adds indirection but no additional clarity.

blocks.content: 10. How Big Is Too Big?
There is no fixed line-count rule for class size. Instead, use these checks:

["One Noun, One Purpose: Can the class be described with a single noun, and do all methods support that purpose? If every method belongs to the same concept, size alone is not a problem.
","One Reason to Change: Would different teams modify this class for different reasons? If unrelated teams can independently request changes, the class likely has multiple responsibilities.
","Easy to Test: Can a feature be tested without mocking unrelated dependencies? If testing pricing requires mocking email or database code, responsibilities are probably tangled.
","Then Look at Size: Only after the previous checks pass should you worry about line count. A large class with one responsibility may be acceptable. A small class with multiple responsibilities is not.
"]
items: One Noun, One Purpose: Can the class be described with a single noun, and do all methods support that purpose? If every method belongs to the same concept, size alone is not a problem.
One Reason to Change: Would different teams modify this class for different reasons? If unrelated teams can independently request changes, the class likely has multiple responsibilities.
Easy to Test: Can a feature be tested without mocking unrelated dependencies? If testing pricing requires mocking email or database code, responsibilities are probably tangled.
Then Look at Size: Only after the previous checks pass should you worry about line count. A large class with one responsibility may be acceptable. A small class with multiple responsibilities is not.

blocks.content: 11. Common Mistakes

Splitting by Size Instead of Responsibility: Don't split a class simply because it has too many lines. Split it based on responsibility boundaries. Two smaller classes with mixed responsibilities are no better than one large class.
Adding Methods Without Re-evaluating Responsibility: A new method may seem harmless, but if it introduces a new dependency or concern, it may belong in a different class.

Misunderstanding the Orchestrator: After extraction, the original class often becomes an orchestrator. Its job is coordinating other classes, not implementing their logic. Avoid moving responsibilities back into it.
Over-Extracting Tiny Classes: Not every method deserves its own class. Creating one-method classes without a clear responsibility adds complexity and navigation overhead.
Trusting Metrics Blindly: Metrics such as LCOM can help identify design problems, but they are only indicators. Good metrics do not guarantee good design.
12. Quick Reference

["Responsibility: A reason for a class to change.
","God Object: A class that has accumulated many unrelated responsibilities.
","Real Measure of Size: Count responsibilities, not lines of code.
","Signs a Class Is Too Big: Too many dependencies, mixed method vocabulary, difficult testing, and unrelated feature changes.
","Signs a Class Is Too Small: Always changes with another class, provides no independent value, and exists only to satisfy a rule.
","Extraction Strategy: Group related methods, extract each responsibility, and leave orchestration behind.
","Rule of Thumb: A class should have one clear responsibility and one reason to change."]
items: Responsibility: A reason for a class to change.
God Object: A class that has accumulated many unrelated responsibilities.
Real Measure of Size: Count responsibilities, not lines of code.
Signs a Class Is Too Big: Too many dependencies, mixed method vocabulary, difficult testing, and unrelated feature changes.
Signs a Class Is Too Small: Always changes with another class, provides no independent value, and exists only to satisfy a rule.
Extraction Strategy: Group related methods, extract each responsibility, and leave orchestration behind.
Rule of Thumb: A class should have one clear responsibility and one reason to change.
